title: Administrator Mindset: Regulation to Real Life
teach: Strong RCFE administration means recognizing risk, verifying the governing rule, acting within scope, documenting objectively, and fixing the system. Use R.E.A.L.: Recognize, Evaluate, Act, Learn & Lead.
hunt: Locate the current RCFE topic that addresses Administrator responsibility. Enter the section/topic and one sentence describing what it requires.
scenario: At 8:05 AM a caregiver reports a resident fall. At 8:07 AM the med tech reports a blank MAR box from yesterday. At 8:09 AM an AM caregiver calls off. At 8:12 AM an LPA arrives.
questions: What should be handled first and why?
What can be delegated to qualified staff?
What records must remain unchanged and truthful?
feedback: Protect and assess the resident first. Delegate appropriate operational tasks to qualified staff, maintain medication safety, and cooperate with Licensing. Never hide, alter, or backdate records. Delegation does not remove Administrator oversight.

quiz.q: Which issue should receive the first immediate response?
quiz.why: Immediate resident health and safety takes priority.

title: Licensing, Incidents & Plans of Correction
teach: Licensing readiness is daily operational readiness. For incidents use: PROTECT → ASSESS → FACTS → NOTIFY/REPORT → DOCUMENT → PREVENT.
hunt: Find the current RCFE incident/reporting topic. Note what facts are needed before deciding what reporting is required.
scenario: A resident with dementia is found in the parking lot outside a side gate. Staff believe an outside provider may have left the gate unsecured, but no one saw the resident exit.
questions: What do you do before investigating the gate?
Which statements are facts versus assumptions?
What systems should be checked?
feedback: Bring the resident to safety and assess first. Build a factual timeline. Do not document an unverified cause as fact. Evaluate required notifications/reporting and correct immediate hazards. A strong Plan of Correction includes owner, deadline, audit, monitoring, and prevention.

quiz.q: What comes first after an unexpected resident exit?
quiz.why: Resident safety precedes root-cause analysis.

title: Medication Safety: Order • Label • MAR
teach: When medication information does not align: STOP → VERIFY → COMMUNICATE → DOCUMENT. Never turn 'I think' into a charted fact.
hunt: Locate the medication-management topic and enter two safeguards related to medication assistance.
scenario: The physician order and pharmacy label match, but yesterday's MAR box is blank. The employee says, 'I'm pretty sure I gave it.' Today's dose is due now.
questions: What do you know for certain?
What do you NOT know?
What should be verified before acting?
feedback: Do not fill in the MAR from memory without a factual basis. Verify the order and available facts, protect the resident from duplicate/missed-dose risk, communicate with the appropriate professional as needed, and document accurately.

quiz.q: Which sequence is safest when medication information conflicts?
quiz.why: Verification and communication should precede unsupported action or charting.

title: Admission, Assessment & Retention
teach: A vacant room does not determine whether a person is appropriate for an RCFE. Admission and retention decisions must be supported by current information about resident needs and facility capability.
hunt: Locate the admission/appraisal and Needs & Services Plan topics and enter one requirement from each.
scenario: A family offers to pay a premium rate if Dad can move in tonight. They say he is mostly independent, but hospital paperwork mentions extensive transfer assistance and current physician information is incomplete.
questions: What facts must be clarified before accepting him?
What staffing or equipment questions matter?
Can financial pressure drive the decision?
feedback: Do not substitute family description or the offered rate for a supported admission decision. Reconcile conflicting information, obtain current assessment/medical information, and determine whether the facility can safely meet needs within RCFE requirements.

quiz.q: What is the best response to incomplete admission information?
choices: Obtain sufficient current information before final commitment
quiz.why: The decision should be supported by current information and facility capability.

title: Dementia: Behavior Is Communication
teach: Instead of asking 'How do we stop this behavior?' ask 'What is this person communicating?' Evaluate baseline, environment, physical need, old routines, relationship/approach, and what works.
hunt: Locate the dementia-care topic and enter two concepts supporting individualized care or safe supervision.
scenario: Every afternoon at 4:30 PM, Mary goes to the front door and says she needs to pick up her children from school. When corrected, she becomes more upset.
questions: What might 4:30 PM represent?
What physical or environmental triggers should be checked?
How could staff respond without arguing?
feedback: Treat the repeated statement as meaningful communication. Explore lifelong routine, time-of-day cues, hunger, fatigue, toileting, anxiety, and environment. Use calm validation/redirection and safe supervision, then update the care plan with what works.

quiz.q: The first question after a repeated dementia behavior should often be:
choices: What might the resident be communicating?
quiz.why: Person-centered dementia care looks for needs, triggers, and meaning.
